title: Hundreds of Workers March in Taipei for Better Pensions
summaryZh: 數百名勞工台北遊行，要求加薪及雇主提撥退休金提高至9%。
summaryHi: ताइपे में सैकड़ों मज़दूरों ने बेहतर पेंशन और ज़्यादा वेतन के लिए मार्च किया।
summaryEs: Cientos de trabajadores marchan en Taipéi para pedir mejores pensiones y salarios.
summaryJa: 台北で数百人の労働者がデモ、年金の雇用主負担引き上げと賃上げを要求。
summaryKo: 타이베이에서 수백 명의 노동자가 연금 개선과 임금 인상을 요구하며 행진했다.
summaryEn: Hundreds of workers marched in Taipei to ask for higher pay and bigger pension payments from employers.
paragraphs: Hundreds of workers took to the streets of Taipei on Monday, demanding higher wages, larger employer pension contributions and clearer rules on how companies share their profits. The marchers represented dozens of labor unions from across Taiwan.

Starting outside the Presidential Office on Ketagalan Boulevard, the protesters walked past the Legislative Yuan before returning. Their central complaint concerns the labor pension scheme introduced in 2005, which requires employers to contribute at least 6 percent of a worker's monthly salary.

Ho Cheng-chia, who chairs the Taiwan Solidarity Front Confederation of Trade Unions, argued that this rate is far too low to fund a decent retirement. He proposed raising it to 9 percent first and gradually to 15 percent, saying it would help make up for 21 years of insufficient contributions. Around 7.87 million workers are covered by the scheme.

The rally comes amid growing labor unrest. Two branches of the Chunghwa Telecom Workers' Union, which has about 20,000 members, have approved strike action, citing record company profits, although the union's chairman said a walkout before the end of the year is unlikely. Another union leader called for a general strike before the 2028 elections if reform stalls.

The Ministry of Labor said it remained open to higher employer contributions but that any change would require careful evaluation. It also noted that the minimum monthly wage will rise from NT$29,500 to NT$30,900 next year.
On Monday, hundreds of workers walked through the streets of Taipei. They came from dozens of workers' groups, called unions, from all over Taiwan.
They started outside the President's office. Then they walked past the building where lawmakers work.

The workers want three things. First, they want higher pay. Second, they want more money for when they stop working and get old. Today, companies must put at least 6 percent of a worker's pay into a pension each month. The workers say this is too little. They want 9 percent first, and later 15 percent.
Third, they want clear rules about how companies share their profits with workers.
Some workers are angry at big companies. At Chunghwa Telecom, workers voted to say they may stop work. The government says it is open to change, but it needs to think carefully.

Hundreds of workers marched through central Taipei on Monday, asking for higher wages, better pensions and clearer rules on sharing company profits. The marchers came from dozens of labor unions across Taiwan.

The protest began outside the Presidential Office on Ketagalan Boulevard and passed the Legislative Yuan before returning. Under Taiwan's labor pension system, which started in 2005, employers must pay at least 6 percent of a worker's monthly salary into a pension account.

Union leader Ho Cheng-chia said 6 percent is too low for people to save enough for retirement. He wants the minimum raised to 9 percent first, and then slowly to 15 percent. About 7.87 million workers are now in the system.

Unions also want the Labor Standards Act changed so that rules on profit-sharing are clearer. At Chunghwa Telecom, two branches of the 20,000-member union have voted to allow a strike, saying the company is making record profits.
The Ministry of Labor said it is open to raising employer payments but that any change needs careful study. The minimum wage will rise to NT$30,900 a month next year.

Hundreds of workers took to the streets of Taipei on Monday, demanding higher wages, larger employer pension contributions and clearer rules on how companies share their profits. The marchers represented dozens of labor unions from across Taiwan.

Starting outside the Presidential Office on Ketagalan Boulevard, the protesters walked past the Legislative Yuan before returning. Their central complaint concerns the labor pension scheme introduced in 2005, which requires employers to contribute at least 6 percent of a worker's monthly salary.

Ho Cheng-chia, who chairs the Taiwan Solidarity Front Confederation of Trade Unions, argued that this rate is far too low to fund a decent retirement. He proposed raising it to 9 percent first and gradually to 15 percent, saying it would help make up for 21 years of insufficient contributions. Around 7.87 million workers are covered by the scheme.

The rally comes amid growing labor unrest. Two branches of the Chunghwa Telecom Workers' Union, which has about 20,000 members, have approved strike action, citing record company profits, although the union's chairman said a walkout before the end of the year is unlikely. Another union leader called for a general strike before the 2028 elections if reform stalls.

The Ministry of Labor said it remained open to higher employer contributions but that any change would require careful evaluation. It also noted that the minimum monthly wage will rise from NT$29,500 to NT$30,900 next year.

Hundreds of workers converged on central Taipei on Monday to press for higher pay, more generous employer pension contributions and greater transparency over profit-sharing. Drawn from dozens of unions nationwide, the marchers set off from Ketagalan Boulevard outside the Presidential Office and filed past the Legislative Yuan.

At the heart of their grievance is the pension scheme launched in 2005, under which employers are obliged to set aside a minimum of 6 percent of monthly wages. Union leader Ho Cheng-chia contended that this falls well short of what is needed for a dignified retirement, and urged the government to lift the floor to 9 percent before gradually raising it to 15 percent.

Ho framed the increase as compensation for two decades of inadequate contributions, noting that employers under the old system typically spent around 12 percent of wages on retirement costs. Roughly 7.87 million employees now have accounts under the newer scheme.

The march reflects a wider mood of labor militancy. Branches of the 20,000-strong Chunghwa Telecom Workers' Union have authorised industrial action over what they describe as record profits, while one regional union chief warned of a general strike ahead of the 2028 elections should reform stall.

The Ministry of Labor said it was 'open' to raising the employer rate but stressed that such a step would require 'careful evaluation', pointing instead to existing incentives and a scheduled rise in the minimum wage to NT$30,900 a month in 2027.

Hundreds of employees marched through Taipei on Monday to demand improved wages, larger pension contributions from employers and clearer regulations on profit-sharing. The demonstration, which brought together dozens of trade unions, highlights growing concern about whether Taiwan's workers can afford to retire.

The central issue is the pension system introduced in 2005. It obliges employers to contribute at least 6 percent of an employee's monthly salary, a rate that union leaders consider inadequate. Ho Cheng-chia, a prominent union figure, proposed increasing the minimum to 9 percent initially and eventually to 15 percent.

Supporters of reform argue that the current level has left millions of people with insufficient savings, particularly as living costs continue to rise. Approximately 7.87 million workers are now covered by the scheme, so even a small change would have a significant impact on both employees and businesses.

The protest also reflects broader tensions between labor and management. At Chunghwa Telecom, union branches have voted to authorise a strike, claiming that employees have not benefited fairly from record profits. Another leader warned that a general strike could take place before the 2028 elections if no progress is made.

In response, the Ministry of Labor stated that it was willing to consider higher contributions, but emphasised that any reform would require careful evaluation of its effects on employers. It also highlighted the planned increase in the minimum wage next year.

protest.ex: Thousands joined the protest in the square.

put.ex: Put aside some money each month.

raising.ex: They are raising funds for the hospital.

rally.en: a large public meeting for a cause

rate.ex: The population is growing at a slow rate.

record.es: registro (on record: desde que hay registros)
record.ex: This was the wettest month on record.

reflects.en: shows or is caused by something

reform.en: a change to improve a system

note.meaning: 改革，指對制度做出改善性的改變。
note.usage: 可當名詞或動詞；常見 public service reform、tax reform。

example.en: The government promised to reform the health system.
example.zh: 政府承諾改革醫療體系。

noteHi.usage: संज्ञा और क्रिया दोनों; tax reform, public service reform।
noteHi.exampleTr: सरकार ने स्वास्थ्य व्यवस्था सुधारने का वादा किया।

noteEs.usage: Sustantivo o verbo: 'reform the system', 'carry out reforms'.
noteEs.exampleTr: El Gobierno prometió reformar el sistema sanitario.

noteJa.meaning: 制度をよくするための変更。
noteJa.usage: 名詞・動詞どちらも可：reform the system。
noteJa.exampleTr: 政府は医療制度の改革を約束した。

noteKo.usage: 명사·동사 모두 가능: reform the system.

noteEn.meaning: A change made to improve a system.
noteEn.usage: Noun or verb: 'reform the system', 'carry out reforms'.

regulations.ex: New regulations will limit noise near schools.

remained.ex: The shop remained open all night.

represented.ex: The figure represented a big rise.

response.ex: The film got a warm response from critics.

retire.en: to stop working because of age
retire.ex: He plans to retire when he turns sixty-five.

retirement.en: the time after you stop working
retirement.ex: She is saving money for her retirement.

returning.ex: The marchers were returning to the square by evening.

rules.en: official instructions about what is allowed
rules.ex: The school has strict rules about phones.

salary.ex: Her salary is paid at the end of each month.

savings.ex: The changes will make big savings.

say.ex: Experts say the plan will work.

saying.ex: He left, saying he was tired.

says.ex: Experts say the plan will work.

scheduled.ex: The meeting is scheduled for Monday.

scheme.ex: The bike scheme is popular in Dublin.

set.en: to put (set aside: keep for later)
set.ex: The government set aside more money.

share.ex: We should share the benefits fairly.

sharing.en: giving part of what you have to others

short.ex: The team fell short of its goal.

significant.ex: There was a significant rise in rents.

note.meaning: 重大的、顯著的，比 big 正式，雅思寫作常用。
note.usage: 副詞 significantly 常用來描述數據變化；名詞 significance。

example.en: There has been a significant rise in house prices.

noteHi.meaning: महत्वपूर्ण, उल्लेखनीय — big से अधिक औपचारिक।
noteHi.usage: क्रियाविशेषण significantly आँकड़ों के लिए उपयोगी।
noteHi.exampleTr: घरों की कीमतों में भारी वृद्धि हुई है।

noteEs.meaning: Importante o notable; más formal que 'big'.
noteEs.usage: Muy útil en IELTS; el adverbio 'significantly' describe cambios en datos.
noteEs.exampleTr: Ha habido una subida notable del precio de la vivienda.

noteJa.meaning: 気づくほど大きい、重要な；big より改まった語。
noteJa.usage: IELTS で便利。副詞 significantly はデータの変化を表す。
noteJa.exampleTr: 住宅価格が大きく上昇した。

noteKo.meaning: 눈에 띌 만큼 크거나 중요한; big보다 격식 있는 말.
noteKo.usage: IELTS에 유용. 부사 significantly는 데이터 변화를 나타낸다.

noteEn.meaning: Large or important enough to notice; more formal than 'big'.
noteEn.usage: Very useful in IELTS writing; adverb 'significantly' describes data changes.

slowly.ex: The car moved slowly in the snow.

small.ex: It's a small town in the west.

so.en: used in 'so far' meaning until now
so.ex: So far, everything is going well.

solidarity.en: unity and support within a group
solidarity.ex: Workers showed solidarity with the striking nurses.

some.ex: Some fifty people came to the meeting.

spent.ex: They spent too much on the party.

stall.ex: Arguments could stall the peace talks.

stalls.ex: If the talks stall, workers may strike again.

standards.en: levels of quality that are expected
standards.ex: The hotel has very high standards.

started.ex: It started to rain after lunch.

starting.en: beginning at a place or time
starting.ex: Starting at the station, the walk takes an hour.

stated.ex: The report stated the facts clearly.

step.ex: The first step is to fill in the form.

streets.ex: The streets were full of tourists.

stressed.en: said strongly that it is important
stressed.ex: She stressed the need for care.

strike.ex: Workers went on strike for better pay.

strong.ex: The company had a strong year.

study.ex: A new study shows the risks.

supporters.en: people who agree with and help an idea
supporters.ex: Supporters of the new park held a meeting.

system.en: a set of rules or ways of working

taiwan.en: an island country in East Asia

take.ex: Many parents will take a day off.

telecom.ex: She works for a telecom company.

tensions.ex: Tensions between the two groups are growing.

example.en: Talks were held to ease tensions between the two sides.
example.zh: 雙方舉行會談以緩和緊張關係。

note.usage: 常見 tensions between A and B；rising tensions；ease/reduce tensions。

noteEn.meaning: a feeling of conflict or distrust between groups.
noteEn.usage: Common: 'tensions between A and B', 'ease tensions'.

noteHi.exampleTr: दोनों पक्षों के बीच तनाव कम करने के लिए बातचीत हुई।
noteHi.meaning: समूहों के बीच तनाव या टकराव।
noteHi.usage: tensions between A and B; ease tensions आम हैं।

noteEs.exampleTr: Se celebraron conversaciones para reducir las tensiones entre ambas partes.
noteEs.usage: Se usa tensions between A and B; ease tensions.

noteJa.exampleTr: 両者の緊張を和らげるため協議が行われた。
noteJa.usage: tensions between A and B、ease tensions の形が多い。

noteKo.exampleTr: 양측의 긴장을 완화하기 위해 회담이 열렸다.
noteKo.usage: tensions between A and B, ease tensions 형태가 흔하다.

things.ex: Put your things in the bag.

think.ex: Experts think a deal is possible.

through.ex: The shop is open Monday through Friday.

today.ex: Today there are fewer than 70 growers.

together.ex: Send the form together with a photo.

too.ex: The coffee is too hot to drink.

took.en: used in 'took part' meaning joined in
took.ex: Everyone took part in the game.

transparency.en: openness so others can see the facts
transparency.ex: Voters want more transparency about public spending.

example.en: Voters want more transparency in public spending.
example.zh: 選民希望公共支出更透明。

note.usage: 常見 greater transparency；lack of transparency；形容詞 transparent。

noteEn.meaning: openness, so that people can see how decisions are made.
noteEn.usage: Common: 'greater transparency', 'lack of transparency'; adjective: transparent.

noteHi.exampleTr: मतदाता सरकारी ख़र्च में ज़्यादा पारदर्शिता चाहते हैं।
noteHi.usage: greater transparency; lack of transparency आम हैं।

noteEs.exampleTr: Los votantes quieren más transparencia en el gasto público.
noteEs.usage: Se usa greater transparency; lack of transparency.

noteJa.exampleTr: 有権者は公的支出の透明性向上を望んでいる。
noteJa.meaning: 透明性；決定過程が見えること。
noteJa.usage: greater transparency、lack of transparency の形が多い。

noteKo.usage: greater transparency, lack of transparency 형태가 흔하다.

typically.ex: Trains are typically late in winter.

union's.ex: The union's rules apply to all members.

unlikely.ex: It is unlikely to rain today.

unrest.ex: Rising prices led to unrest among workers.

urged.en: strongly asked someone to do something
urged.ex: The doctor urged him to stop smoking.

voted.en: made a choice in a vote
voted.ex: Most members voted for the plan.

wage.ex: The minimum wage rose this year.

wages.ex: The minimum wage rose this year.

walkout.en: a strike where workers leave work
walkout.ex: The pilots staged a walkout over pay.

well.ex: She speaks Irish as well as English.

where.ex: This is the town where I grew up.

whether.en: used to express a choice (if or not)

wider.ex: The benefits should reach the wider city.

will.en: used to talk about the future
will.ex: The new bridge will open next year.

willing.ex: He is willing to help us.

work.ex: Robots can do some hard work.

worker's.ex: The worker's pay rose by five percent.

workers.ex: Public sector workers want higher pay.

would.ex: A new park would help the town.

yuan.en: a branch of Taiwan's government, as in Legislative Yuan
